q: In which language was the Kama Sutra originally written?
note: 'Kama' means desire or pleasure; 'sutra' means a thread, or a string of aphorisms.

q: Who published the famous 1883 English translation of the Kama Sutra with F. F. Arbuthnot?
note: They dodged Victorian obscenity laws by printing it privately under a 'Kama Shastra Society' label.

q: The Kama Sutra lists 64 arts a cultured person should learn. Which of these makes the list?
note: Singing, dancing, cooking and carpentry also make the list. Not all 64 happen in the bedroom.

q: Into how many parts, or books, is the Kama Sutra divided?
note: Only one part is mainly about sex; others cover wooing, marriage, courtesans and even love potions.

q: Which medieval Indian love manual did the poet Kalyanamalla write in honour of a nobleman named Lad Khan?
note: Unlike the Kama Sutra, it is aimed at keeping married couples happy together.

q: Kokkoka's medieval Indian love manual 'Ratirahasya' is popularly known by what other name?
note: 'Ratirahasya' roughly means 'secrets of passion'.

q: In the Kama Sutra, what is a 'nagaraka'?
note: The text describes his daily routine: bathing, perfumes, chewing betel and evening parties.

q: Which 1996 English-language period film set in 16th-century India borrowed its title from an ancient Indian text?
a: Kama Sutra: A Tale of Love
options: Kama Sutra: A Tale of Love

q: The Khajuraho temples, famous for their erotic carvings, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in which year?
note: Erotic scenes are only a small share of the carvings; most show daily life, musicians and dancers.

q: Which British army engineer is credited with bringing the Khajuraho temples to wider attention in 1838?
In which month is the annual Khajuraho Dance Festival usually held?
note: Classical dancers perform against the floodlit temples as a backdrop.

q: In which year did India's Supreme Court decriminalise gay sex between adults by reading down Section 377?
note: The unanimous verdict came on 6 September from a five-judge Constitution Bench.

q: What is the name of the landmark case in which India's Supreme Court read down Section 377?
a: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
options: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
M. C. Mehta v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
note: Justice Indu Malhotra wrote that history owed the LGBTQ+ community an apology.

q: Which Chief Justice of India headed the bench that read down Section 377?
Which High Court first decriminalised gay sex in India in 2009, before the Supreme Court reversed it in 2013?
note: That 2009 case was brought by the Naz Foundation, an HIV/AIDS charity.

q: India's 2017 Puttaswamy judgment, which paved the way for the Section 377 verdict, declared which fundamental right?
note: The judges called sexual orientation an essential attribute of this right.

q: In Joseph Shine v. Union of India, the Supreme Court struck down the colonial-era law criminalising what?
note: The court said a husband is not the master of his wife.

q: Section 377 belonged to which criminal code, drafted in British India?
note: It was enacted in 1860 and came into force in 1862.

q: In October 2023, what did India's Supreme Court decline to do?
note: The court said it was for Parliament to decide.

q: In which 1964 case did India's Supreme Court uphold a bookseller's obscenity conviction over 'Lady Chatterley's Lover'?
a: Ranjit D. Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra
options: Kharak Singh v. State of U.P.
Sakal Papers v. Union of India
Ranjit D. Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra
Bennett Coleman v. Union of India
note: In 2014 the court swapped that old Victorian obscenity test for contemporary community standards.

q: What was the name of India's first LGBTQ+ magazine, launched in 1990?
note: Its founder, journalist Ashok Row Kavi, was one of India's first openly gay public figures.

q: Which LGBTQ+ health and rights organisation did journalist Ashok Row Kavi found in 1994?
Which Indian state set up the country's first welfare board for trans people, in 2008?
note: It was first named the Aravanigal Welfare Board.

q: KASHISH, a long-running queer film festival, is held in which city?
note: It began in 2010.

q: Deepa Mehta's 1996 film about two sisters-in-law who fall in love is titled what?
note: It is the first part of her 'Elements' trilogy, followed by 'Earth' and 'Water'.

q: Ismat Chughtai was tried for obscenity over which 1942 Urdu short story hinting at a romance between two women?
note: 'Lihaaf' means 'The Quilt'; she fought the obscenity case and won.

q: The 1933 film 'Karma' is famous for an early on-screen kiss featuring which actress?
note: Her co-star in that kiss was her real-life husband.

q: Moods condoms are made by which government-owned healthcare company?
note: It began life in 1966 as Hindustan Latex Limited.

q: Which Marathi reformer opened one of India's first birth-control clinics, in Bombay in 1921?
note: His Marathi magazine 'Samaj Swasthya' discussed sex and family planning frankly for decades.

q: Which symbol has long represented family planning in India?
note: You'd spot it on clinics and health posters across the country.

q: Complete India's classic family-planning slogan: 'Hum Do, ___'.
note: It translates to 'We two, our two'.

q: India became the first country with a national family planning programme. In which year was it launched?
India's first HIV infections were detected in 1986 in which city?
note: Microbiologist Dr Suniti Solomon and her student Sellappan Nirmala made the discovery.

q: In which year was India's National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) set up?
Which of the nine rasas of classical Indian aesthetics is the rasa of love and desire?
note: It is often praised as 'rasaraja', the king of rasas.

q: Ancient Indian texts list 64 refined arts, from music to perfumery, known as the 'chatushashti ___'.
Classical Indian love poetry sorts its heroines into eight types, the 'ashta-___'.
note: Each type reflects a different mood of love, from eager waiting to jealous sulking.

q: Classical Tamil Sangam poetry is split into puram, about war and public life, and which genre about love?
note: Akam poems never name their lovers, keeping the romance universal.

q: Which playwright wrote the classical Indian play 'Mrichchhakatika', whose heroine is the courtesan Vasantasena?
note: Its title means 'The Little Clay Cart'.

q: Which fruit, cut in half, was reportedly used by 18th-century lovers as an early cervical cap?
note: Don't try this at home: modern methods are far more reliable, and far less stingy.

q: Which fruit's name traces back to the Aztec Nahuatl word 'ahuacatl', which also meant 'testicle'?
note: Spanish speakers turned it into 'aguacate' before English made it the word we know.

q: Old British slang called a condom a 'French ___'.
note: The French returned the favour, calling it an 'English hood'.

q: The oldest surviving condoms, found at an English castle, date to which century?
note: They were made from animal intestine, long before rubber arrived.

q: Which American nurse opened America's first birth-control clinic in 1916?
note: She popularised the very phrase 'birth control'.

q: Marie Stopes, who opened Britain's first birth-control clinic in 1921, wrote which 1918 bestseller?
Which 1873 US law made it a crime to mail contraceptives or information about them?
note: It was named after anti-vice crusader Anthony Comstock.

q: The US Supreme Court's 1965 Griswold v. Connecticut ruling protected married couples' right to use what?
note: Unmarried couples won the same right in a follow-up case in 1972.

q: A roughly 28,000-year-old polished stone phallus, possibly the oldest known sex toy, was found in which country?
note: Archaeologists think it may also have doubled as a flint-knapping tool.

q: Which Roman poet wrote 'Ars Amatoria' ('The Art of Love'), a cheeky guide to seduction?
note: Rome's emperor exiled him in 8 CE, reportedly partly over this poem.

q: Which Roman poet wrote passionate love poems to a woman he called 'Lesbia'?
note: 'Lesbia' was probably a pen name for a real aristocrat, Clodia.

q: Which ancient Roman festival featured fertility rites, with runners playfully striking onlookers with goat-hide strips?
note: Being struck was believed to boost fertility and ease childbirth.

q: What were ancient Roman 'tintinnabula'?
note: These bronze bells were hung in doorways and gardens for good luck.

q: In ancient Greece, who were the 'hetairai'?
note: Aspasia, partner of the Athenian statesman Pericles, is often described as one.

q: Traditionally, Japanese geisha were trained mainly as what?
note: Their name roughly means 'person of the arts'.

q: In Edo-period Japan, what were the high-ranking courtesans, often confused with geisha, called?
note: Their slow, elaborate parades through the pleasure quarters drew huge crowds.

q: Chinese Emperor Ai of Han inspired the phrase 'passion of the cut sleeve'. What did he do?
a: Cut off his sleeve rather than wake his lover
options: Cut off his sleeve rather than wake his lover
Sewed his lover a silk robe
Cut his hair as a keepsake
Burned a sleeve of love letters
note: His lover, Dong Xian, had fallen asleep on the emperor's sleeve.

q: 'Jin Ping Mei', a famously explicit Ming-dynasty novel, is known in English as 'The Plum in the Golden ___'.
note: It was banned for long stretches, yet is celebrated as a masterpiece of Chinese fiction.

q: Sheikh Nefzaoui's 15th-century Arabic sex manual is known in English as 'The Perfumed ___'.
In medieval Europe, what was the idealised, often secret romance between a knight and a noble lady called?
note: Troubadours spread its songs of longing across 12th-century France.

q: In French culture, the early-evening 'cinq à sept' has long been a playful code for what?
note: The phrase literally means 'five to seven', the hours after work and before dinner.

q: Veronica Franco was a celebrated 16th-century poet and courtesan in which Italian city?
note: She published poetry and even petitioned for a home for poor women.

q: Diane de Poitiers was the powerful long-time mistress of which French king?
note: Henry wore her colours, black and white, for the rest of his life.

q: Actress Nell Gwyn was the famous long-time mistress of which English king?
note: Before the stage, she reportedly sold fruit to theatre audiences.

q: British naval hero Horatio Nelson had a famously public affair with which woman?
note: Both were married to other people at the time, which only fuelled the gossip.

q: Which American socialite did a British king give up his throne to marry?
note: The couple married in France in 1937.

q: Dancer Lola Montez's scandalous affair helped topple which Bavarian king in 1848?
note: He had made her a countess, which infuriated his ministers.

q: Which 18th-century Russian empress had a famous romance with her adviser Grigory Potemkin?
note: Some historians believe the pair secretly married in 1774.

q: Which French novelist had a nearly decade-long affair with composer Frédéric Chopin?
note: She famously wore men's clothing and smoked in public.

q: Which poet did Elizabeth Barrett secretly marry in 1846, against her father's wishes?
note: Their love letters, nearly 600 of them, still survive.

q: Lady Caroline Lamb famously described her lover Lord Byron as 'mad, bad and ___ to know'.
note: She wrote it in her journal after first meeting him in 1812.

q: 'Lothario', a word for a seducer, comes from a character in which playwright's 1703 play 'The Fair Penitent'?
The word 'pander' comes from Pandarus, a lovers' go-between in tales set during which war?
note: Shakespeare put him on stage in 'Troilus and Cressida'.

q: Which English metaphysical poet wrote the seductive poem 'To His Coy Mistress'?
note: Its speaker argues that life is far too short for playing hard to get.

q: Who wrote 'The Well of Loneliness', the 1928 lesbian novel banned in Britain?
note: A British court ordered copies destroyed; it was republished there only after her death.

q: Anne Lister, whose coded diaries recorded her relationships with women, lived at Shibden Hall in which English county?
note: The TV series 'Gentleman Jack' dramatised her life.

q: An 1896 short film of a couple kissing, among cinema's first on-screen kisses, came from which inventor's company?
note: Its 18-second smooch caused a moral outcry.

q: Which German entrepreneur opened what is considered the world's first sex shop, in Flensburg in 1962?
note: She had earlier worked as a stunt pilot.

q: The Hitachi Magic Wand, later famous as a vibrator, was launched in 1968 as what?
note: Sex educator Betty Dodson's workshops later helped make it a feminist icon.

q: Which Victorian British doctor patented an early electromechanical vibrator in the 1880s, meant for aching muscles?
note: Historians still argue over how such devices were actually used on patients.

q: What did psychoanalyst Wilhelm Reich call the 'life energy' his cabinet-like accumulators supposedly collected?
note: Mainstream science never found any evidence that it exists.

q: Which men's magazine did Hugh Hefner launch in 1953?
note: The first issue carried no date, as Hefner doubted there would be a second.

q: Which pharmaceutical company launched Viagra?
note: Its scientists at Sandwich, in Kent, England, developed the drug.

q: In which decade did the US FDA first approve a female condom?
note: It can be inserted up to eight hours before sex.

q: Pre-rubber style condoms made from animal intestine, still sold today, are usually marketed under what name?
note: They help prevent pregnancy, but viruses like HIV can slip through.

q: In the 1920s, which young women famously shocked elders with short skirts, jazz and 'petting parties'?
The 1967 hippie gathering in California's Haight-Ashbury, a symbol of the sexual revolution, is remembered as the what?
note: An estimated 100,000 young people poured into the neighbourhood.

q: Before 'gay' came to mean homosexual, what did the word usually mean in English?
note: The word came into English from the Old French 'gai'.

q: The terms 'heterosexual' and 'homosexual' were coined in the 1860s by which Hungarian-born writer?
What does the French phrase 'ménage à trois' literally mean?
What does 'femme fatale' literally mean in French?
What does the Latin phrase 'amor vincit omnia' mean?
note: It comes from the Roman poet Virgil.

q: Which law partly decriminalised sex between men in England and Wales in 1967?
note: Other parts of the UK followed in the early 1980s.

q: Which country became the first to open civil marriage to same-sex couples, in 2001?
note: Four couples tied the knot in the very first ceremonies on 1 April 2001.

q: In 1989, which country became the first to legally recognise same-sex couples through registered partnerships?
note: Activists Axel and Eigil Axgil were among the first couples registered.

In 2006, which became the first African country to let same-sex couples marry?
